summary: Defines a MIB module for modeling TE links as described in Link Bundling in MPLS Traffic Engineering. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: A manager needs a dashboard for bundled links. This memo defines the readouts and switches for it.

questions: what is the te link mib
what is a bundled link in mpls
subtitle: An SNMP MIB module for configuring and monitoring traffic engineering links and bundled links.

tldr.problem: Traffic engineering (TE) links and bundled links, defined for MPLS and GMPLS, need a standard way to be configured and monitored by network management systems.
tldr.mechanism: The TE-LINK-STD-MIB module defines tables for TE links, their descriptors, shared risk link groups, priority-based bandwidth and component links. It plugs into the Interfaces Group by giving TE links their own interface type.
tldr.outcome: Operators get SNMP objects for both configuration and performance monitoring of TE links. The module is rooted at { transmission 200 }.

today: RFC 4220 is a Proposed Standard. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of the TE-LINK-STD-MIB.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
OSPF (RFC 3630), GMPLS (RFC 3471) and the Link Management Protocol (RFC 4204) use TE links to abstract link properties. This reduces the routing information exchanged in the network, which improves routing scalability, and allows new capabilities such as link protection.

This document defines a MIB module to manage TE links and their extension, the bundled link. It supports both configuration and performance monitoring. The objects are derived from the link bundling document, RFC 4201. The module is written in SMIv2 and is accessed through SNMP, as part of the Internet-Standard Management Framework (RFC 3410).
sections.eli5: A big road made of several lanes can be described as one road. This memo gives managers a standard way to look at and set up such roads.

sections.title: TE Links, Bundles and Component Links
sections.content:
A TE link is a subinterface that can carry MPLS traffic engineered traffic. It may consist of only one underlying component link. A bundled link is another kind of TE link: a subinterface that binds the traffic of a group of one or more TE links. There should be more than one TE link in a bundle, but this is not required. If all but one are deleted later, the agent may delete the bundle or leave it intact. Traffic counters on a bundle are cumulative for all subinterfaces it binds.

The terminology comes from link bundling (RFC 4201) and the GMPLS architecture (RFC 3945).
sections.eli5: Component links are single lanes. A TE link groups lanes, and a bundled link groups those groups into one big road.

sections.title: The MIB Tables
sections.content:
Seven tables make up the data model. Four describe TE links: teLinkTable (the links, including bundled links, and their generic TE parameters), teLinkDescriptorTable (interface switching capability descriptors), teLinkSrlgTable (shared risk link groups, or SRLGs) and teLinkBandwidthTable (priority-based bandwidth parameters). Three describe component links: componentLinkTable, componentLinkDescriptorTable and componentLinkBandwidthTable.

Component links in the same TE link must be compatible, and TE links in a bundle must have compatible resource class, link metric and protection type. Some TE link bandwidth values (maximum reservable bandwidth, minimum LSP bandwidth, maximum LSP bandwidth at a priority, unreserved bandwidth) are derived from the component link values.

The module defines textual conventions for bandwidth (a 4-octet IEEE floating point value, in bps, used to allow large numbers rather than fractions), priority (0 is highest, 7 is lowest), switching capability, encoding type and SONET/SDH indication. Priority-based tables carry a bandwidth entry per priority.
sections.eli5: The MIB is a set of seven tables of facts: one set about the groups and one set about the single lanes inside them.

sections.title: Setting Up a Bundled Link
sections.content:
The RFC walks through building a bundled link from two 1:1 TE links, with SRLGs 10 and 50 and port entity interfaces (lambdas) as component links. The order is: create the bundled link entry (an ifEntry of type teLink must already exist), create the two TE links, assign SRLGs to the TE links, then create a component link for each unbundled TE link. Each step also adds a row to the ifStackTable to record which interface sits on which.

The bundled link inherits SRLG properties from its TE links. Component link descriptors are added implicitly when a component link is created, and TE link descriptors are derived from them. The devices maintain the bandwidth attributes as LSPs are created and deleted at different priorities.
sections.eli5: You build the big road from the bottom: first the lanes, then the groups, then the whole road. Each piece is written down in a table.

sections.title: Fitting Into the Interfaces Group
sections.content:
A TE link is represented as an entry in ifTable (RFC 2863), with ifType teLink(200). Relationships between interfaces are shown in ifStackTable. In the RFC's example, an MPLS interface (ifType 166) sits on a bundled TE link, which sits on two TE links, each on a component link of type opticalTransport(196). If MPLS uses a single TE link, the bundle layer is not needed.

For the ifTable, ifSpeed is the total bandwidth in bits per second for the TE link layer, ifPhysAddress is unused, and ifLinkUpDownTrapEnable defaults to disabled. Octet counters are cumulative over the component links. TE links are logical interfaces with no media-level addresses, so ifRcvAddressTable does not apply.
sections.eli5: Every TE link is listed like any other network port, and a stacking table shows which port sits on top of which.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Objects with read-write or read-create access can be sensitive. All tables in this module hold routing information, so unauthorized changes can disrupt resource allocation in the network. Readable objects can also be sensitive: the local and remote IP addresses in teLinkTable may reveal a provider's internal address space.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not have adequate security. Implementers are RECOMMENDED to use the SNMPv3 security features, including cryptographic authentication and privacy, and deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED. Operators must make sure only legitimate principals can GET or SET the objects.
sections.eli5: These settings control how traffic flows, so only trusted people should be allowed to change or even peek at them.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The TE-LINK-STD-MIB is rooted under the transmission subtree. IANA assigned { transmission 200 } to the module. The MIB module itself records its initial version as dated 11 October 2005 and published as RFC 4220.
sections.eli5: The module got its own official number so it never clashes with anyone else's.
